Building Sahabat-AI with Seven Indonesian Universities

By Furaihan Kamyl Arnazaye · 2024–2025 · 4 min read
In short
  • Sahabat-AI is an open-source LLM from GoTo and Indosat, built for Indonesian, Sundanese, Javanese, Batak, and Balinese.
  • I led the university program: seven universities contributing training data, research capacity, and interns.
  • Every engagement ran end to end, from account management and negotiation to running the events.
  • To source informal Indonesian, GoTo supported a Lentera App writing competition for dialogue-heavy urban short stories, used with creator consent.
  • I also made sure the training data did not infringe intellectual property rights.

"Gak begitu, njir."

Some version of that sentence is sitting in almost every Indonesian's phone right now. It also appears in almost no formal corpus, no academic publication, and no dataset that a large language model would ordinarily be trained on.

Indonesia has hundreds of living languages, millions of daily conversations in slang and regional dialects, and a digital economy that runs on informal communication. Most large language models are trained predominantly on English data, and when they do support Indonesian, they support the formal written version of it. Sahabat-AI was GoTo's answer to that gap. My part in it was the university collaboration program.

Sahabat-AI is an open-source Large Language Model developed by PT GoTo Gojek Tokopedia Tbk in collaboration with PT Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison, trained specifically for Bahasa Indonesia and regional languages, currently supporting Indonesian, Sundanese, Javanese, Batak, and Balinese. The premise was clear from the start. Indonesia's AI future should be built from Indonesian language and context rather than retrofitted from Western models. Development involved local universities, media groups, language communities, and global research partners including AI Singapore.

Building the University Program

I led the university collaboration program, which meant building and managing the partnerships that contributed training data, research capacity, and digital talent to the project. Seven universities were involved:

  • Universitas Indonesia (UI)
  • Universitas Gadjah Mada (UGM)
  • Institut Pertanian Bogor (IPB)
  • Institut Teknologi Bandung (ITB)
  • Universitas Sumatera Utara (USU)
  • Universitas Hasanuddin (Unhas)
  • Universitas Udayana

Each partnership was structured around several forms of collaboration. Training data contribution by faculty and students. Student internship programs for AI data training work. Knowledge-sharing sessions paired with MOU or PKS signings. At Universitas Indonesia, an AI research grant program on top of that.

What made this complex was that every engagement ran end to end. Account management, then negotiation, then event project management, which was the part I had the least preparation for. I learned the technical nuances on the job. Invitation management, university crowd coordination, session design for a mixed student and faculty audience, and hospitality standards that nobody notices when they are met and everybody notices when they are not. A campus that feels used by a company does not sign the next agreement.

Sourcing the Language Nobody Writes Down

The most unconventional part of Sahabat-AI's data strategy was a collaboration with Lentera App, a local literary platform, built to collect informal Indonesian language data that formal sources could not provide.

Slang, abbreviations, and natural conversational Indonesian are extremely difficult to source from existing publications and academic literature. Phrases like "Kalo gw liat-liat, si. Gk ada, ya." fill every Indonesian's text messages and appear nowhere in a formal corpus. So we went looking for them somewhere else.

The solution was a writing competition focused on urban short stories written in conversational, dialogue-heavy language. Participants submitted work that naturally produced the informal, textured Indonesian the model needed. GoTo served as a supporter, and the collected works, with creator consent, became part of the training dataset. To my knowledge, that was one of the more creative approaches to the data sourcing problem in Indonesian AI development.

That consent clause is where my other responsibility sat. As a PPGR professional embedded in this initiative, my work extended into policy compliance, specifically ensuring that the training data used in Sahabat-AI's development did not infringe intellectual property rights. That meant working through the legal frameworks around data consent and verifying that university and community contributions were rights-free, openly licensed, or explicitly consented to by their creators. AI training data ethics is still an evolving conversation, and there was no settled standard to copy. Building the check into the process from the start was a legal necessity, and I think it was also the right way to build something meant to serve Indonesian society.

Sahabat-AI is an argument that Indonesian language, regional diversity, and local talent are sufficient and necessary inputs for building AI that actually works for Indonesia.

Indonesia's AI sovereignty should be built from within.

I am glad to have been part of building that foundation.
